vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. A foreign national generally can buy and own a home in Los Angeles; U.S. citizenship, a green card, or California residency is not generally required simply to purchase residential property. The practical requirements differ considerably depending on whether you're paying cash or obtaining a U.S. mortgage.

For a typical purchase, you'll generally need:

- Identification: A valid foreign passport is commonly used, plus whatever identity documentation the escrow/title company requires.
- Funds: You'll need to document and transfer the purchase funds through escrow. Banks, escrow companies, and lenders may require substantial documentation concerning the source of funds for compliance purposes.
- U.S. bank account: Not necessarily a legal requirement to own the property, although having one can make escrow, mortgage payments, property taxes, HOA fees, and other expenses much easier.
- ITIN: You don't necessarily need an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number merely to acquire property, but an ITIN can become important for U.S. tax filings and eventually selling the property. The IRS specifically provides ITIN procedures for foreign persons in connection with U.S. real estate taxation. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai))
- Mortgage qualification, if financing: This is often the biggest difference for foreign buyers. A lender may offer a "foreign national" mortgage without U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, but underwriting can require a larger down payment and documentation of foreign income, assets, bank statements, and creditworthiness. California's DRE notes generally that lenders consider credit history, employment stability and down payment when qualifying buyers. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/consumers/informationforhomebuyers.html?utm_source=openai))
- Escrow/title: California purchases normally involve escrow and title work. A preliminary title report identifies ownership, liens and other encumbrances, and title insurance can protect against specified title defects. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/Consumers/FirstHomeCalifornia.html?utm_source=openai))

There are also some important issues that foreign buyers should plan for before choosing how to hold title.

Buying personally versus through an LLC, corporation, or trust can have very different U.S. income-tax and estate-tax consequences for a non-U.S. person. That's one area where I'd recommend getting advice from a U.S. international-tax attorney or CPA before closing rather than deciding based only on privacy or liability considerations.

There has also been a recent change concerning federal reporting of certain all-cash purchases through entities and trusts. FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Rule was vacated by a federal court on March 19, 2026, and FinCEN says that, as of September 2026, reporting persons are currently not required to file the Real Estate Reports contemplated by that rule while the court order remains in effect. The government has appealed. ([fincen.gov](https://www.fincen.gov/rre?utm_source=openai))

Finally, buying a Los Angeles home does not, by itself, give the purchaser U.S. immigration status or a right to live in the United States. Immigration status and property ownership are separate matters.

One significant tax issue comes later when a foreign owner sells. Under FIRPTA, dispositions of U.S. real estate by foreign persons are generally subject to federal withholding rules, with the buyer usually acting as the withholding agent. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai)) California has its own real-estate withholding rules as well. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2026/2026-593-instructions.html?utm_source=openai))

If you're asking for yourself, I can also lay out exactly what you'd need for a Los Angeles purchase based on, for example, "Chinese citizen, no green card, $2M home, 40% down" or "UK citizen buying all-cash through an LLC."
